raw_response.country: Global review with emphasis on Brazil (including comparative discussion of the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and Japan)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) service access and emergency provision (public bathrooms, mobile toilets and showers, temporary handwashing stations, and shelter/hotel sanitation) for people experiencing homelessness during the COVID-19 pandemic.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this paper would satisfy Criterion 2 (plain = yes) because it examines legal, institutional, and governance factors including Brazil's National Policy for the Homeless Population (Federal Decree No. 7.053/2009), state and municipal COVID-19 emergency decrees, decentralized crisis governance, policy fragmentation, and public funding priorities. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, however, it fails Criterion 2 (narrow = no) because it focuses on macro-governance arrangements (decentralization, interinstitutional coordination gaps, funding allocation toward emergency cash aid rather than WASH infrastructure, and lack of Housing First policy integration) and emergency project/service delivery (mobile toilets/showers, hygiene kits, temporary hotel shelters) rather than analyzing a specific rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure; criminalization of public space is mentioned only as a brief secondary citation in Table 3). Note that plain_criterion2_decision is still 'exclude' because the paper independently fails Criterion 3 (E05).
criterion_notes.c3: No primary empirical WASH access data and not a systematic empirical synthesis (exclude E05). The study conducts an integrative review and documentary policy analysis of 94 sources (retaining 94 of 95 retrieved records), of which 61.7% are non-peer-reviewed institutional reports (30/94), governmental laws/decrees/plans (20/94), and grey literature/technical notes/blogs/news pieces (9/94), alongside 36 peer-reviewed articles. Rather than collecting primary empirical data on homeless populations' WASH access or systematically synthesizing empirical study designs and access effect/mechanism evidence, it classifies how the 94 documents frame WASH across four thematic axes and provides a narrative critical policy commentary.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report primary empirical outcomes or systematically synthesized empirical outcomes of population-level WASH access, connection, availability, continuity, quantity, or affordability. Its own data output measures document-level thematic frequencies ('inequality of attention' across four analytical axes of the 94 documents), supplemented only by brief narrative descriptions and secondary citations regarding emergency mobile/hotel WASH interventions.
criterion_notes.c5: While the documentary review methods are described, the unit of analysis for the authors' coding is the policy/literature document (n = 94 heterogeneous global and Brazilian sources), and the paper does not report study-level empirical populations, rule-type exposures, and measured WASH access outcomes suitable for empirical or socio-legal mechanism synthesis.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English, an eligible language without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing on an integrative review and documentary analysis of 94 sources, evidence was categorized across four analytical axes: Immediate Access, Equity and Inclusion, Sustainability and Political Integration, and Social Context.

Therefore, this article aims to critically analyze the policies and measures adopted internationally and, more specifically, within the Brazilian context concerning access to water, sanitation, and healthcare for people experiencing homelessness during the COVID-19 pandemic.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 5 (Distribution and nature of publications)
evidence_quotes.quote: Peer-reviewed scientific articles accounted for 38.3% of the included references (36/94), whereas institutional reports represented 31.9% (30/94). Governmental legal and regulatory documents – including laws, decrees, emergency plans, and strategic frameworks – comprised 21.3% (20/94), while technical reports, technical notes, and other forms of grey literature accounted for the remaining 9.6% (9/94).

Immediate interventions comprised the deployment of mobile toilets and shower facilities, the installation of temporary handwashing stations, the distribution of hygiene kits, and the implementation of hotel-based isolation and shelter programs.

Despite the existence of a national normative framework in Brazil, the operationalization of pandemic responses remained largely decentralized and dependent on the capacities and priorities of state and municipal governments.

raw_response.exposure: COVID-19 WASH and public health policy responses, including national normative frameworks (Brazil Federal Decree No. 7.053/2009), decentralized state and municipal emergency decrees, and temporary emergency interventions (hotel sheltering, mobile toilets and showers, handwashing stations, and hygiene kits)
raw_response.outcome: Thematic framing and institutional prioritization ('inequality of attention') across 94 reviewed documents categorized into four analytical axes (Social Context, Sustainability and Political Integration, Immediate Access to WASH, and Equity and Inclusion), alongside narrative policy assessment
raw_response.population_and_sample: People experiencing homelessness (topic population); analyzed documentary sample of 94 sources (36 peer-reviewed articles, 30 institutional reports, 20 governmental legal and regulatory documents, and 9 technical reports or grey literature sources)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence), with an additional fail on Criterion 2 under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type scope. The paper is a predominantly policy-oriented integrative review and documentary analysis of 94 sources (94 of 95 retrieved items retained, over 60% consisting of governmental decrees/laws, institutional reports, technical notes, and blogs/commentary) that categorizes how documents thematically frame WASH during COVID-19 rather than reporting primary empirical WASH access data or conducting a systematic synthesis of empirical studies. Furthermore, although it passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 by discussing national and municipal decrees and pandemic governance, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because it examines macro-level crisis governance (decentralization, fragmentation, funding gaps) and emergency service delivery (mobile showers/toilets, hotel shelters, hygiene kits) rather than a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing WASH service access. Because it lacks primary empirical access evidence and is not a systematic empirical synthesis, plain_criterion2_decision is also 'exclude'.
raw_response.study_design: Integrative review and documentary policy analysis (n = 94 documents)
